title: 25 Boring Businesses That Quietly Make Millionaires

scenes.text: Hi, I'm Ryan Rover. When people imagine getting rich from a business, they picture tech startups, apps and venture capital. But a lot of quiet millionaires in America made their money doing something much less exciting. Washing cars. Storing boxes. Killing bugs. Pumping septic tanks. Boring businesses. And boring, it turns out, can be beautiful.
scenes.caption: RYAN
scenes.short_hook: The most boring businesses in America quietly make millionaires. Here are twenty five.

scenes.text: Twenty five boring businesses. No apps, no hype, no viral videos. Just services people need, again and again, whether the economy is booming or not.

Here's why boring works. Boring businesses usually solve a problem people can't or won't solve themselves. They often have repeat customers. Many are local, so a giant tech company can't easily take them over. And because they're not glamorous, there's often less competition from people chasing the next big thing.
scenes.caption: WHY BORING WORKS

scenes.text: Back in the nineteen nineties, Thomas Stanley and William Danko wrote The Millionaire Next Door. They found that many American millionaires were self employed, and many of them ran what the authors called dull, normal businesses: contractors, pest control, cleaning, welding, and more. Not famous. Not flashy. Just profitable for a long time.
scenes.caption: THE MILLIONAIRE NEXT DOOR

scenes.text: In this video, twenty five of those businesses: how they make money, and what to watch out for. Then we'll look at the whole idea from three angles. The numbers behind small business. The psychology of the owners who succeed. And a playbook for starting or buying one, without betting everything you have.
scenes.caption: 25 BUSINESSES, 3 ANGLES

scenes.text: One honest warning first. No business is guaranteed to make money, and many small businesses fail. This video is about understanding the models, not about promises. Let's go.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Small business counts come from the U.S. Small Business Administration's Office of Advocacy. Business survival rates come from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Wage figures for skilled trades come from the Bureau of Labor Statistics Occupational Outlook Handbook. Where we give example numbers for a business, they're simple illustrations, not industry averages, because results vary enormously by location, management and luck. This is education, not financial or business advice.
scenes.caption: OUR SOURCES

scenes.text: Angle one. The numbers. Let's look at the reality of small business in America before we get excited.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: The SBA Office of Advocacy counts more than thirty three million small businesses in the United States. They employ nearly half of all private sector workers.

Thirty three million. That's a lot of businesses, and the vast majority have no employees at all. They're one person operations: a consultant, a handyman, a freelance bookkeeper. Most small businesses aren't trying to become the next big company. They're trying to give their owner a good living and, eventually, something valuable to sell.
scenes.caption: MOSTLY ONE PERSON

scenes.text: And that's the key mindset shift for this whole video. A boring business doesn't have to become huge to change your life. A single well run location, route or service area that pays its owner a solid income and builds value over twenty years can be the difference between retiring on a modest salary and retiring as a millionaire.
scenes.caption: IT DOESN'T HAVE TO BE HUGE

scenes.text: But survival is hard. Bureau of Labor Statistics data shows roughly one in five new businesses close within their first year, and about half are gone within five years.

card.note: Bureau of Labor Statistics, Business Employment Dynamics (approximate)

scenes.text: So why talk about boring businesses at all? Because the failure rate isn't spread evenly. Businesses with proven demand, simple operations and repeat customers tend to have better odds than brand new ideas that need to convince people they want something. A plumber doesn't need to convince anyone that pipes break. Demand is already there.
scenes.caption: PROVEN DEMAND

scenes.text: And the reward can be big. The Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances has consistently found that families who own a business tend to have a much higher median net worth than families who don't. Business ownership is one of the main paths to wealth in America, alongside real estate and long term investing. It's riskier, but it's also one of the few paths where your upside isn't capped by a salary.
scenes.caption: OWNERS HAVE MORE WEALTH

scenes.text: So what makes a boring business good? Look for five traits. One, demand that doesn't depend on trends. People need clean clothes, working pipes and no termites in any decade. Two, recurring revenue: customers who pay every week, month or season instead of once. Three, a local moat, meaning the work happens in a physical place, so a website on the other side of the world can't easily take your customers.
scenes.caption: TRAITS 1 TO 3

scenes.text: Four, a reason most people avoid it. Dirty, smelly, physical, or simply unglamorous work keeps competition lower than in businesses everyone dreams about. And five, a path to systems. The best boring businesses can eventually run with a manager and a team, so the owner earns from the business instead of being the business. When you look at each of the twenty five businesses in this video, check how many of these five traits it has.
scenes.caption: TRAITS 4 AND 5

scenes.text: And here's one more number worth knowing. Many owners of established service businesses say the hardest part isn't finding customers. It's finding and keeping good workers. In the skilled trades especially, demand for qualified people has been strong. That's a challenge if you're an owner, but it's also an opportunity if you're thinking about learning a trade first, getting paid while you learn how the business really works.
scenes.caption: THE REAL BOTTLENECK

scenes.text: Okay. Twenty five boring businesses. We'll start with the ones that run on machines, because machines don't call in sick.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Business number one. Laundromats.
scenes.caption: BUSINESS 1

scenes.text: Millions of Americans don't have a washer and dryer at home, especially renters in apartments. They need to wash clothes every week, no matter what the economy is doing. A laundromat sells machine time, plus extras like wash and fold service, vending, and sometimes pickup and delivery. Many owners run them with few or no full time staff.
scenes.caption: WEEKLY DEMAND

scenes.text: What to watch: machines are expensive, and a lease, water and utility costs can eat profits. Location is everything, ideally near dense apartment housing. Many people buy an existing laundromat rather than build one, and look closely at the age of the machines and the remaining years on the lease before signing anything.
scenes.caption: LOCATION AND LEASE

scenes.text: Business number two. Car washes.

card.title: Car washes
card.sub: dirty cars never go out of style

scenes.caption: BUSINESS 2

scenes.text: Car washes range from self serve bays to fully automated tunnels. A big trend in recent years has been monthly memberships: customers pay a flat fee for unlimited washes, which creates predictable, recurring revenue. Automated washes can serve a lot of cars per hour with a small team.
scenes.caption: MONTHLY MEMBERSHIPS

scenes.text: What to watch: building a modern tunnel wash can cost millions, and competition has grown as investors have poured into the industry. Water, equipment repairs and weather all affect results. Smaller self serve washes cost less to buy, but usually earn less too. Study local competition carefully.
scenes.caption: WATCH THE COMPETITION

scenes.text: Business number three. Self storage.
scenes.caption: BUSINESS 3

scenes.text: Americans have a lot of stuff, and they move, downsize, divorce, renovate and inherit. Self storage rents small spaces month by month. Once a facility is full, costs are relatively low: some staff, security, maintenance and marketing. Many customers stay much longer than they planned.
scenes.caption: STUFF PAYS RENT

scenes.text: What to watch: building a facility takes land and serious capital, and new supply in an area can push prices down. Large public companies dominate in many cities. Smaller investors often look at buying existing facilities in growing towns, or converting old buildings.
scenes.caption: CAPITAL AND COMPETITION

scenes.text: Business number four. Vending machines.
scenes.caption: BUSINESS 4

scenes.text: Vending is one of the easiest businesses to start small. You buy a machine, place it in a location like an office, a gym or a factory, often sharing a cut with the location owner, and restock it regularly. Modern machines accept cards and phones, and some send sales data so you only restock when needed.
scenes.caption: START SMALL

scenes.text: What to watch: profits per machine are often modest, so the business only becomes meaningful with many machines and efficient routes. Good locations are competitive. Machines can be damaged or stolen. Treat online claims of huge passive income from one machine with a lot of skepticism.
scenes.caption: ROUTES MATTER

scenes.text: Business number five. ATM machines.
scenes.caption: BUSINESS 5

scenes.text: Independent ATM owners place machines in bars, convenience stores, events and other spots where people need cash. Each withdrawal earns a surcharge fee, often split with the location. Once a machine is installed, the main jobs are keeping it filled with cash and running.
scenes.caption: A FEE EVERY TIME

scenes.text: What to watch: cash use has been declining as cards and phones take over, which is a real long term risk. You need cash to load the machines, and security matters. Like vending, this business usually only works at scale, with many machines in busy locations.
scenes.caption: CASH IS DECLINING

scenes.text: Next, the trades and home services. These are the businesses Stanley and Danko kept finding among quiet millionaires.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Business number six. Plumbing.
scenes.caption: BUSINESS 6

scenes.text: When a pipe bursts, nobody shops for the cheapest option. They call someone who can come now. Plumbing combines emergency work, renovations and new construction. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported a median pay for plumbers of around sixty three thousand dollars a year in twenty twenty four, and owners who build a team can earn much more.
scenes.caption: PIPES ALWAYS BREAK

scenes.text: What to watch: it takes years of training and licensing, which is also what protects good plumbers from competition. Growing beyond yourself means hiring, managing and finding skilled workers, which many trades owners say is the hardest part of the business.
scenes.caption: HIRING IS THE HARD PART

scenes.text: Business number seven. Heating, ventilation and air conditioning.
scenes.caption: BUSINESS 7

scenes.text: Every home and commercial building needs heating and cooling, and systems break, age out and need regular maintenance. Many HVAC companies sell maintenance plans, which create recurring revenue and steady customers. Demand spikes in heat waves and cold snaps.
scenes.caption: EVERY SEASON

scenes.text: What to watch: like plumbing, HVAC needs licensed technicians and training, and the busy seasons can be exhausting. Equipment costs and changing efficiency regulations matter. Owners who build strong maintenance plan programs often have the most stable businesses.
scenes.caption: MAINTENANCE PLANS

scenes.text: Business number eight. Electrical contracting.
scenes.caption: BUSINESS 8

scenes.text: Electricians wire new homes, upgrade old panels, install EV chargers and solar systems, and fix problems. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported a median pay for electricians of around sixty two thousand dollars in twenty twenty four, and projects demand for the trade to keep growing as buildings electrify.
scenes.caption: ELECTRIFICATION

scenes.text: What to watch: licensing takes years, and the work carries real safety risk. Contracting businesses depend on construction cycles, so a housing slowdown can hurt. Many electrical contractors balance new construction with service work to smooth out the ups and downs.
scenes.caption: BALANCE THE CYCLES

scenes.text: Business number nine. Pest control.
scenes.caption: BUSINESS 9

scenes.text: Termites, ants, roaches, rodents. Pest control is a classic boring business, and one of the most recurring. Many customers sign up for quarterly or monthly service. Real estate transactions often require termite inspections, which adds steady demand.
scenes.caption: RECURRING SERVICE

scenes.text: What to watch: you need state licensing to apply many chemicals, and safety and regulations matter. Big national brands compete in many markets. Smaller operators often win on service and local reputation, and some build routes that they eventually sell to larger companies.
scenes.caption: LOCAL REPUTATION

scenes.text: Business number ten. Landscaping and lawn care.
scenes.caption: BUSINESS 10

scenes.text: Lawns grow every week in the season, and many homeowners and businesses would rather pay someone than mow. You can start with a mower and a trailer. Over time, businesses add services like design, irrigation, tree work and snow removal in winter.
scenes.caption: GRASS KEEPS GROWING

scenes.text: What to watch: the barrier to entry is low, so competition is high and prices can be pressured. It's physical work, and it's seasonal in many places. The owners who do well often focus on commercial contracts and recurring residential routes, not one time jobs.
scenes.caption: ADD WINTER WORK

scenes.text: Business number eleven. Septic pumping and portable toilets.
scenes.caption: BUSINESS 11
scenes.short_hook: Nobody wants to pump septic tanks. That's exactly why it can pay so well.

scenes.text: Around one in five American homes uses a septic system, according to the Environmental Protection Agency, and tanks need regular pumping. Portable toilets are needed at every construction site, festival and outdoor event. These businesses are the definition of unglamorous, which keeps a lot of people away.
scenes.caption: 1 IN 5 HOMES

scenes.text: What to watch: trucks and equipment are expensive, and there are environmental regulations on disposal. But demand is steady and recurring, and many owners say that the very thing that makes it unappealing, the smell, is what protects them from competition.
scenes.caption: UNGLAMOROUS = LESS COMPETITION

scenes.text: Business number twelve. Junk removal.

card.title: Junk removal
card.sub: people pay you to take their stuff

scenes.caption: BUSINESS 12

scenes.text: Moving, renovations, estate cleanouts, office clear outs. People pay to make things disappear. A truck, a couple of strong workers and good reviews can get you started. Some items can be donated, recycled or resold, which adds a bit of extra income.
scenes.caption: TAKE IT AWAY

scenes.text: What to watch: dump fees, fuel and labor are the big costs. Franchises compete in many cities. Success often comes from great reviews, fast scheduling, and relationships with real estate agents and property managers who need cleanouts regularly.
scenes.caption: REAL ESTATE RELATIONSHIPS

scenes.text: Business number thirteen. Commercial cleaning.
scenes.caption: BUSINESS 13

scenes.text: Offices, clinics, gyms and schools need cleaning, often every night. Commercial contracts can be monthly and recurring, which makes revenue predictable. Many owners start by cleaning themselves, then hire teams as they win more contracts.
scenes.caption: RECURRING CONTRACTS

scenes.text: What to watch: margins depend on managing labor well, and staff turnover can be high. Winning contracts takes bidding and relationships. The owners who succeed usually build reliable systems and quality checks, so clients never have a reason to switch.
scenes.caption: SYSTEMS AND QUALITY

scenes.text: Business number fourteen. Pressure washing.

card.title: Pressure washing
card.sub: low start up, high visual impact

scenes.caption: BUSINESS 14

scenes.text: Driveways, decks, siding, storefronts, parking lots. The results are dramatic, which makes marketing easy: before and after photos sell themselves. Start up costs are relatively low compared with many businesses.
scenes.caption: BEFORE AND AFTER

scenes.text: What to watch: low barriers mean lots of competition. Damage to property is a real risk if you don't know what you're doing, so training and insurance matter. Commercial clients, like restaurants and property managers, can provide steadier recurring work than one time homeowners.
scenes.caption: COMMERCIAL CLIENTS

scenes.text: Business number fifteen. Pool cleaning and maintenance.
scenes.caption: BUSINESS 15

scenes.text: Pool owners in warm states need weekly cleaning, chemical balancing and equipment repairs. A route of regular customers creates recurring monthly income. Repairs and equipment replacements add higher value jobs on top.
scenes.caption: A ROUTE OF REGULARS

scenes.text: What to watch: it's seasonal in colder areas, and chemicals require care and knowledge. Some owners build routes and later sell them to larger operators. Good communication with customers is what keeps routes from shrinking.
scenes.caption: ROUTES CAN BE SOLD

scenes.text: Quick pause. If you'd like a deeper video on any of these businesses, tell me which one in the comments. And subscribe, because the next videos in this series go into the real numbers: laundromats, car washes, storage units, and how to buy a business instead of starting one. Now, business sixteen.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Business number sixteen. Auto repair.
scenes.caption: BUSINESS 16

scenes.text: Americans are keeping their cars longer, and S and P Global Mobility has reported the average age of cars and light trucks on U.S. roads at a record of more than twelve and a half years. Older cars need more repairs. Independent shops that earn trust can keep customers for decades.
scenes.caption: OLDER CARS, MORE REPAIRS

scenes.text: What to watch: cars are getting more complex, with electronics and electric vehicles requiring new tools and training. Finding good technicians is a challenge. Shops that invest in diagnostics and build a reputation for honesty tend to thrive.
scenes.caption: TRUST IS EVERYTHING

scenes.text: Business number seventeen. Towing.
scenes.caption: BUSINESS 17

scenes.text: Breakdowns, accidents, illegally parked cars, repossessions. Towing companies often have contracts with police departments, property managers and roadside assistance programs, which create steady volume.
scenes.caption: CONTRACTS MATTER

scenes.text: What to watch: trucks are expensive, insurance is costly, and the work can be dangerous and around the clock. Regulations vary by city. Strong contracts with clubs, insurers and local businesses often matter more than random calls.
scenes.query: Car with flat tire on road
scenes.caption: 24/7 WORK

scenes.text: Business number eighteen. Dumpster rental.
scenes.caption: BUSINESS 18

scenes.text: Contractors, roofers, renovators and homeowners cleaning out a house all need roll off dumpsters. You drop it off, pick it up, and dispose of the contents. Repeat contractor customers can provide steady volume.
scenes.caption: EVERY PROJECT MAKES TRASH

scenes.text: What to watch: trucks and containers require capital, and landfill fees and fuel are major costs. Local relationships with contractors are the core of the business. Pricing carefully for weight and distance protects profits.
scenes.caption: WATCH LANDFILL FEES

scenes.text: Business number nineteen. Bookkeeping and tax preparation.
scenes.caption: BUSINESS 19

scenes.text: Every small business needs bookkeeping, and millions of households pay someone to do their taxes. Monthly bookkeeping clients create recurring revenue. Tax season brings a big wave of work every year.
scenes.caption: MONTHLY CLIENTS

scenes.text: What to watch: you need skills and accuracy, and certain services require credentials. Software has automated parts of the work, so the best firms focus on advice and service, not just data entry. Busy season can mean very long hours.
scenes.caption: TAX SEASON

scenes.text: Business number twenty. Funeral homes.
scenes.caption: BUSINESS 20

scenes.text: It's a hard topic, but demand is certain. Funeral homes are often family owned for generations, and trust and reputation in a community are everything. Services include planning, preparation, cremation and pre need contracts.
scenes.caption: CERTAIN DEMAND

scenes.text: What to watch: licensing is required, buildings and vehicles are expensive, and the shift toward cremation has changed revenue for many funeral homes. The emotional side of the work is demanding. Consolidators buy independent funeral homes in many markets.
scenes.caption: TRUST AND REPUTATION

scenes.text: Business number twenty one. Mobile home parks and RV parks.
scenes.caption: BUSINESS 21

scenes.text: In many mobile home parks, residents own their homes but rent the land underneath. Moving a manufactured home is expensive, so residents tend to stay for many years. RV parks earn from travelers and long term stays.
scenes.caption: RENT THE LAND

scenes.text: What to watch: these businesses have faced criticism over rising lot rents, and some states have strengthened tenant protections. Infrastructure like water and sewer can be costly to maintain. Investors who do this well treat residents fairly and keep parks safe and well run.
scenes.caption: TREAT RESIDENTS FAIRLY

scenes.text: Business number twenty two. Parking lots.

card.title: Parking lots
card.sub: a lot that earns while it sits

scenes.caption: BUSINESS 22

scenes.text: In busy downtowns, near stadiums, airports and hospitals, parking is in demand. A lot can earn steady income with simple operations, especially with automated payment systems.
scenes.caption: LAND THAT EARNS

scenes.text: What to watch: land in good locations is expensive. Remote work and ride sharing have changed demand in some cities. Many lot owners see the land itself as a long term investment, with parking income paying the bills while they wait.
scenes.caption: LOCATION, LOCATION

scenes.text: Business number twenty three. Window and gutter cleaning.
scenes.caption: BUSINESS 23

scenes.text: Homes need gutters cleaned once or twice a year. Storefronts want clean windows every week or month. It's simple work with low start up costs, and customers who are happy tend to book again and again.
scenes.caption: REPEAT CUSTOMERS

scenes.text: What to watch: ladder work has real safety risks, so training and insurance are essential. It's seasonal in some areas. Offering maintenance plans and bundling services like pressure washing can smooth out revenue.
scenes.caption: SAFETY FIRST

scenes.text: Business number twenty four. Tire shops.
scenes.caption: BUSINESS 24

scenes.text: Every car needs new tires every few years, plus rotations, balancing and repairs. Tire shops often add oil changes, alignments and brakes. With older cars on the road, demand for maintenance stays steady.
scenes.caption: RUBBER WEARS OUT

scenes.text: What to watch: inventory takes capital and space, and big chains compete on price. Local shops win on service and speed. Building relationships with fleets, like delivery companies and contractors, can provide steady volume.
scenes.caption: FLEET CUSTOMERS

scenes.text: Business number twenty five. Sign and print shops.

card.title: Sign and print shops
card.sub: every business needs to be seen

scenes.caption: BUSINESS 25

scenes.text: Every new business needs a sign, banners, vehicle wraps, menus and business cards. Real estate agents need yard signs. Events need banners. It's a steady, local, business to business service.
scenes.caption: EVERY BUSINESS NEEDS SIGNS

scenes.text: What to watch: equipment is an investment, and online printers compete on simple products. Local shops win on custom work, installation and speed. Relationships with contractors, agents and new businesses are the lifeblood.
scenes.caption: LOCAL RELATIONSHIPS

scenes.text: Here's something most people don't understand about boring businesses. The biggest payday usually isn't the yearly profit. It's what the business is worth when you sell it.
scenes.caption: RYAN
scenes.chapter: Where the millions really come from
scenes.short_hook: Most business owners don't get rich from profits. They get rich when they sell.

scenes.text: Small businesses are often valued as a multiple of their yearly profit, sometimes called seller's discretionary earnings. A small service business might sell for something like two to four times its yearly earnings, depending on the industry, how stable it is, and how much it depends on the owner. These are rough ranges, and every deal is different.
scenes.caption: A MULTIPLE OF PROFIT

scenes.text: So imagine a pest control company that earns two hundred thousand dollars a year for its owner. At three times earnings, it might sell for around six hundred thousand dollars. Now imagine the owner spends five years building recurring contracts, training a manager, and documenting everything, and profit grows to three hundred fifty thousand. At a higher multiple, because it no longer depends on the owner, the business might be worth well over a million.
scenes.caption: FROM $600K TO $1M+

scenes.text: That's the hidden math of boring businesses. Every dollar of steady, recurring profit can add several dollars to what the business is worth. And the things that raise the multiple are the same things we talked about: recurring customers, systems, clean records, and an owner who isn't doing every job personally.
scenes.caption: EVERY $1 OF PROFIT = SEVERAL $ OF VALUE

scenes.text: This is why many owners in these industries say the goal is to build something you could sell, even if you never do. A business that depends entirely on you is really a job you own. A business that runs on systems is an asset, and assets are what create millionaires.
scenes.caption: A JOB OR AN ASSET?

scenes.text: Let's make it concrete with three example owners. They're made up, but their paths are common in these industries.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Owner one, Luis. Luis started pressure washing on weekends with about three thousand dollars of equipment. After a year, he had enough repeat customers to quit his warehouse job. He added gutter cleaning and window washing, hired two workers, and focused on restaurants and property managers who needed regular service. Eight years later, his small company gives him a solid income, and he works mostly on sales and scheduling, not on the ladder.
scenes.caption: LUIS: STARTED SMALL

scenes.text: Owner two, Karen. Karen spent twenty years in corporate accounting. Instead of starting from scratch, she used savings and a small business loan to buy an existing laundromat with good records and a long lease. She replaced the oldest machines, added wash and fold and pickup service, and raised revenue steadily. She kept her emergency fund and retirement accounts untouched, so the business was a calculated risk, not a bet on everything.
scenes.caption: KAREN: BOUGHT PROVEN

scenes.text: Owner three, Darnell. Darnell trained as an HVAC technician, worked for a larger company for six years, and learned how the business really ran: pricing, scheduling, maintenance plans, hiring. When he started his own company, he already had skills, customers who trusted him, and a plan. Within a decade, he had several technicians and hundreds of maintenance plan customers.
scenes.caption: DARNELL: LEARNED FIRST

scenes.text: Three different paths. Luis started small with almost no money. Karen bought a proven business with her savings. Darnell learned the trade and the business first, then went out on his own. What they share is patience, careful money management, and a focus on recurring customers. None of them got rich fast. All of them built something real.
scenes.caption: THREE PATHS

scenes.text: Before you start or buy any business, watch for these red flags.
scenes.caption: RYAN
scenes.chapter: Red flags before you jump in

scenes.text: Red flag one. Someone selling a course or a business opportunity that promises passive income with little work. Many online pitches for vending, ATMs or car washes make money mostly by selling the dream, not by running the business. Red flag two. A seller who can't show clean financial records and tax returns. If the numbers aren't documented, assume they're not real.
scenes.caption: RED FLAGS 1 AND 2

scenes.text: Red flag three. A business where all the customers are tied to the owner personally. When the owner leaves, the customers might too. Red flag four. A short lease, or a landlord who won't commit to renewing. Your location could disappear. Red flag five. Old equipment that will need expensive replacement soon after you buy.
scenes.caption: RED FLAGS 3 TO 5

scenes.text: And red flag six. Your own plan requires everything to go right. If the business only works with perfect revenue, no repairs and no slow months, it's too fragile. Build in room for things to go wrong, because they will. The owners who survive are the ones who planned for bad months while things were good.
scenes.caption: RED FLAG 6: NO ROOM FOR ERROR

scenes.text: Angle two. The psychology. Because the business is only half the story. The other half is the owner. What do people who succeed with boring businesses have in common?
scenes.caption: RYAN
scenes.short_hook: The people who get rich from boring businesses share these five traits.

scenes.text: First, they don't need the business to be exciting. They get their excitement from results, from a growing customer list and a healthy bank account, not from telling people at parties what they do. If you need your business to impress strangers, boring businesses will feel painful. If you care about profits and freedom, they can feel wonderful.
scenes.caption: RESULTS OVER IMAGE

scenes.text: Second, they think in systems. The owners who build real wealth don't do every job forever. They write down how the work is done, train people, and build routines so the business can run without them on site every hour. That's what turns a job into an asset someone might want to buy one day.
scenes.caption: SYSTEMS

scenes.text: Third, they're patient. Many boring businesses take years to build a customer base and a reputation. There's no overnight success. But the reward for patience is a business with loyal customers and steady cash flow, which is exactly what makes it valuable.
scenes.caption: PATIENCE

scenes.text: Patience also shows up in how they grow. Instead of borrowing heavily to expand fast, many successful owners add one truck, one route, or one location at a time, funded mostly by profits. It's slower, but it means one bad year doesn't sink the whole company. Growing at the speed of your cash flow is one of the oldest and safest rules in small business, and boring business owners tend to follow it closely.
scenes.caption: GROW AT THE SPEED OF CASH

scenes.text: Fourth, they're careful with money. Successful owners tend to reinvest profits, avoid unnecessary debt, and keep a cash cushion for slow months. Stanley and Danko noticed that many of the business owner millionaires they studied lived well below their means, even after they became wealthy.
scenes.query: Calculator and pen on financial papers
scenes.caption: CAREFUL WITH MONEY

scenes.text: And fifth, they obsess over customers. In local service businesses, reputation is everything. Online reviews, word of mouth, showing up on time. The owners who win treat every customer like they'll be telling ten friends, because they often do.
scenes.caption: CUSTOMERS FIRST

scenes.text: Angle three. The playbook. If one of these businesses interests you, here's how to explore it without risking everything.
scenes.caption: RYAN
scenes.short_hook: Here's how to get into a boring business without betting your life savings.

scenes.text: Step one. Keep your foundation. Before you put money into any business, have an emergency fund, no high interest debt, and your retirement savings going. A business is a risk, and risk should never threaten your family's basic security.
scenes.caption: STEP 1: KEEP YOUR FOUNDATION

scenes.text: Step two. Learn the business from the inside. Work in it, even part time, before you own it. Talk to owners in other cities who won't see you as competition. Ask what surprised them, what their biggest costs are, and what they'd do differently. Most owners love talking about their business.
scenes.caption: STEP 2: LEARN FROM INSIDE

scenes.text: Step three. Start small or buy proven. You can start with low cost services, like pressure washing, cleaning or lawn care, and test demand with almost no risk. Or you can buy an existing business with real customers and records. Both are usually safer than building something big from scratch.
scenes.caption: STEP 3: SMALL OR PROVEN

scenes.text: Step four. Do the math honestly. Revenue isn't profit. List every cost: equipment, insurance, fuel, labor, rent, licenses, taxes, and your own time. If the business only works when you work eighty hours a week for free, it's not a business yet. It's a hard job.
scenes.caption: STEP 4: HONEST MATH

scenes.text: Step five. Protect yourself. Form the right legal structure, get proper insurance, and keep business and personal money completely separate. A good accountant and, when buying, a lawyer, are worth their fees many times over.
scenes.caption: STEP 5: PROTECT YOURSELF

scenes.text: And step six. Build to sell, even if you never sell. Keep clean records, build systems, train people, and grow recurring revenue. Those are the things that make a business valuable to a buyer, and they're also the things that let you take a vacation without everything falling apart.
scenes.caption: STEP 6: BUILD TO SELL

scenes.text: Let me answer the questions people ask most about boring businesses.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Question one. Which one is the best? There's no single best. The best business for you depends on your skills, your money, your location and what you can tolerate. Someone who loves physical work might thrive in landscaping. Someone who likes numbers might prefer bookkeeping or vending routes.
scenes.caption: WHICH ONE IS BEST?

scenes.text: Question two. Are these businesses really passive? Mostly no. Vending, laundromats and storage are often called passive, but they still need management, repairs and attention. Passive usually means you've hired someone else to do the active part. Question three. How much money do I need? Some services start with a few thousand dollars of equipment. Others, like car washes or storage, can cost millions.
scenes.caption: IS IT PASSIVE?

scenes.text: Question four. Should I buy a franchise? Franchises offer a proven system and brand, but come with fees and rules. Read the franchise disclosure document carefully, and talk to current and former franchise owners before signing. Question five. Will AI replace these businesses? Many of them involve physical work in specific places, which is much harder to automate than office work. That's part of their appeal.
scenes.caption: FRANCHISE? AI?

scenes.text: Question six. Can I run one of these while keeping my job? Some, yes. Vending routes, small cleaning contracts, pressure washing on weekends, or a laundromat with a good manager can be started alongside a job. It's often the smartest way to test a business, because your salary covers your life while the business proves itself. Just be honest about your time and energy, and check your employment contract for conflicts.
scenes.caption: KEEP YOUR JOB?

scenes.text: Question seven. Should I use my retirement savings to buy a business? Be very careful. There are complex arrangements that allow it, but they carry real risks and rules, and if the business fails you could lose both your business and your retirement. Most people are better off using savings outside retirement accounts, a small business loan, or seller financing, where the seller lets you pay part of the price over time.
scenes.caption: USE RETIREMENT MONEY?

scenes.text: Let's recap. The machine businesses: laundromats, car washes, self storage, vending machines and ATMs. The trades: plumbing, HVAC, electrical, pest control and landscaping. The jobs nobody wants: septic, junk removal, commercial cleaning, pressure washing and pool service.
scenes.caption: BUSINESSES 1 TO 15

scenes.text: Then auto repair, towing, dumpster rental, bookkeeping and tax prep, and funeral services. And the land and local businesses: mobile home and RV parks, parking lots, window and gutter cleaning, tire shops, and sign and print shops.
scenes.caption: BUSINESSES 16 TO 25

scenes.text: And the three angles. The numbers: tens of millions of small businesses, about half survive five years, but owners tend to build much more wealth. The psychology: results over image, systems, patience, careful money and obsession with customers. And the playbook: keep your foundation, learn from the inside, start small or buy proven, do honest math, protect yourself, and build to sell.
scenes.caption: NUMBERS, PSYCHOLOGY, PLAYBOOK

scenes.text: And here's the bigger lesson behind all twenty five businesses. Wealth often hides in plain sight, in the services everybody uses and nobody thinks about. The laundromat on the corner. The pest control truck in your neighbor's driveway. The company that pumps the septic tank at the edge of town. Behind many of them is an owner who saw a boring, steady need, served it well for years, and quietly built something worth far more than a salary. You don't need a brilliant idea. You need a real need, a lot of patience, and the discipline to run it well.
scenes.caption: WEALTH IN PLAIN SIGHT

scenes.text: And if owning a business isn't for you, that's completely fine too. You can still benefit from the same idea. Broad index funds make you a part owner of thousands of businesses, boring and exciting alike. Owning, in one form or another, is how most wealth gets built. The question is just which form fits your life.
scenes.query: New York Stock Exchange trading floor
scenes.caption: OWNERSHIP, ANY FORM

scenes.text: So here's your homework. Pick two businesses from this list that fit your skills and your budget. This week, call one owner and ask them about their business. That one conversation will teach you more than a hundred videos, including this one. Ask what they love about it, what they hate about it, and what they wish they'd known on day one. If you want the full plan for building wealth, it's in my playbook, link in the description. I'm Ryan Rover. See you in the next one.
scenes.caption: RYAN
